➜ INTRO
The Bronze Bow, winner of the 1962 Newbery Medal, is set in Galilee during the time of Jesus's ministry (approximately 28–33 AD). Galiliee had occupied by Rome for almost 100 years when the story takes place, and the people longed for freedom from Roman oppression. As we read the story, we'll explore both the Galilee region and the culture of Rome during this time period.

➜ READ, NARRATE, & DISCUSS
Read: CHAPTER 1
• Why do you think Daniel trusts Joel and Malthace so quickly?
• What would you miss most if you had to leave your home?

➜ MAPWORK:
• Find Galilee on p. \_\_\_ of your Bible Atlas or [on this map](https://enterthebible.org/map/first-century-galilee/). Notice that Galilee was an area near the Sea of Galilee, not the name of a city. (The name Galilee Hebrew word galil, which translates to "district," "circle," or "region".) 
• Now locate the Sea of Galilee and the town of Caperneum. This was the town the twins said they were moving to. 
• Much of the story takes place in the village of Ketzah, but this is a fictitious town. In the book it is said to be on the northern shore of the Sea of Galilee, three miles from Capernaum. Can you estimate about where this would have been located on your map?

Under Roman law, enslaved people had no rights and were regarded as the property of their masters. They could be bought, sold, and mistreated at will. They were unable to own property, enter into a contract, or legally marry.

➜ RECAP

➜ BACKGROUND
Daniel had run away from Amalek, a cruel blacksmith, where he was a bonded servant. A bonded servant worked for a master, usually to learn a trade or to pay off debt, for a set number of years. Although biblical law mandated protections for indentured Hebrew servants, Amalek treated Daniel cruelly. Unable to endure the abuse, Daniel broke his bond and fled into the mountains making him a runaway and a fugitive from justice.

Daniel's grandmother mentions a "pauper's share" of grain in this chapter. This Biblical practice was called gleaning. Land owners were to leave the edges of their fields unharvested so that the poor and widows could gather the grain to feed themselves. This wasn't a handout - it took a lot of work to gather the grain, seperate it, grind it, and turn it into a course flour to make bread! Do you remember any Bible stories than mention gleaning?

Look closely for details on how the Jewish Sabbath is observed during this chapter. The Sabbath would have been observed from Friday night to Saturday night. Sabbath comes from the Hebrew word _shabbat_, which literally translates to "to rest" or "to cease".

➜ INTRO
In this chapter, Daniel travels to the city of Capernaum. Nestled on the northern shore of the Sea of Galilee, Capernaum was a prosperous fishing village and busy hub of daily life in first-century Galilee. Its rich waters and location along major trade routes made it a natural gathering place. It was also the home base of Jesus during his years of ministry.

Also mentioned in this chapter, Tiberias was built around 20 AD by Herod Antipas and named for the reigning Roman Emperor. Situated along the western shore of the Sea of Galilee near 17 natural hot springs, it served as the Roman capital of Galilee and was meant to show off Roman life. Its construction over an ancient cemetery made it ritually unclean under Jewish law. This initially kept observant Jews away, though it later became a major center of Jewish scholarship.

⍞ Materials: Redemption: The Church in Ancient Times, Historical Atlas of the World

➜ INTRO
In the Bronze Bow, you read a historical fiction book about what was happening in the land of Israel during the time of Jesus around 30 AD. This book tells true accounts of the Christians who lived in the 1st century and carried on the message of Jesus after he ascended into heaven. The events in this book take place from 30 AD to 350 AD. This was still a time when the Romans controlled all the areas around the Mediterranean Sea. All the people you will meet lived in Roman occupied territories. Let's first look at a map to understand what the Roman Empire looked like at this time.

➜ MAP QUESTIONS
⍞ Map Resource: Historical Atlas of the World p.16-17

2.What country was furthest north in the Roman Empire? (Britain)
3.What walls were built near the northernmost part of the Roman Empire? (Wall of Hadrian and Wall of Antoninus)
4.What country was furthest south in the Roman Republic? (Egypt)
5.What country was furthest west in the Roman Republic? (Spain)
6.What country was furthest east in the Roman Republic? (Osroene)

8.Find Jerusalem. That is where the apostles were after the ascension of Jesus.

Forty days after the resurrection and tens days after Jesus ascended to heaven, about 120 followers of Christ gathered together in Jerusalem to celebrate a Jewish feast that had been celebrated since the Old Testament.

Find Antioch on the east side of the Mediterranean Sea. Why do you think that location would be a good place for trade and the spread of Christianity? Antioch was one of the largest cities in the first-century Roman world, accommodating a population between 100,000 and 300,000. There was a thriving church there made up of Jews and Gentiles and Paul had stayed there for a whole year ministering to the people. (Acts 11) Trace a sea route to Rome that stays close to the coast.

➜ INTRO
We will read about Ignatius who was bishop of Antioch (modern-day Turkey) for forty years, probably from AD 67–106. At this time, it was the policy of the Roman government to not to seek out Christians, but still to punish them when they were brought before the authorities. "Once accused and brought before the authorities, Christians had to be forced to worship the gods of the empire, or face punishment...Since great festivities were being planned in Rome in celebration of a military victory, Ignatius was sent to the capital so that his death might provide entertainment for the people. On his way to martyrdom, he wrote seven letters that are among the most valuable documents informing our knowledge of early Christianity" (Justo Gonzalez, The Story of Christianity).

Cyprian
⍞ Materials: Redemption: The Church in Ancient Times

➜RECAP
What did you remember about Polycarp?

➜ LOCATE
⍞ Map Resource: Historical Atlas of the World p.16-17
Find Carthage (F7) Where is it located? (In Africa on the Mediterranean Sea.)

➜ INTRO
Cyprian was the bishop of the church in Carthage from 248 to 258 AD. His writings and teachers have been beneficial to Christians. He helped Christians navigate the question: Do we let people who denied Christ under the threat of torture and death back into the church if they repent?

➜ BACKGROUND
In AD 250 the most violent persecution the church had yet faced was instigated by the emperor Decius (249–51). Decius was determined to have no nonsense from Christians. In his eyes, they were enemies of the empire. Their atheism was responsible for the many troubles in the realm. Thus Decius commanded all citizens of the empire to sacrifice to the traditional Roman gods. Those who did so were given certificates (libelli in Latin) as evidence that they had obeyed the order. Those who refused to comply and were unable (or unwilling) to obtain false libelli from sympathetic or corrupt officials faced death. To save their lives, many Christians complied. Others were able to obtain certificates without having actually sacrificed. But an unknown number of Christians were imprisoned or executed—among them the bishops of Rome, Antioch, and Jerusalem. (Church History in Plain Language)

➜ READ, NARRATE, & DISCUSS
p.63-78 Stop at "a different approach."

• How important is it for Christians to be part of a church body and to attend church regularly? What do you think Cyprian was saying about that topic?
• Why do you think there was disagreement on whether those who denied their faith should be let back in the church?

➜ VIEW
This is a mosaic that is on the wall in a church in Ravenna, Italy that was constructed in the 6th century. A mosaic is a pattern or image made of small regular or irregular pieces of colored stone or glass held in place by plaster and covering a surface. Mosaics are often used as floor and wall decoration, and were particularly popular in the ancient Roman world. On this wall is a procession of martyrs walking from the king's palace towards Christ's throne in heaven. In the other image you can the inside of the church. Polycarp was also represented in this mosaic.

➜ INTRO
When Diocletian became emperor, he thought the empire too large for one man to manage, and for that reason divided different sections out to assistant emperors. When he grew old and retired, the assistant emperors began to quarrel, and their sons as well. Constantine was the son of one, Maxentius was the son of another. Constantine held Britain and Gaul (France). Maxentius held Rome and Italy. Constantine wanted to conquer Maxentius and take control of Rome. We will read about what happened during that battle that finally brought an end to the persecution of Christians.

➜ READ, NARRATE, & DISCUSS

➜ VIEW
∞ Image Link: Chi-Ro Symbol used in ancient Roman Empire
Emperor Constantine used the Chi-Rho symbol on his shields and coinage after his conversion and it was used as a Christian symbol for many centuries on tomb stones, mosaics, cups, tiles and manuscripts. It is made from two Greek letters (Χ and ρ). They are the first two letters of the word Christ and this symbol came to represent Christ, or Christianity.

➜ INTRO
Athanasius is an important person from church history who lived from 293-373 in Alexandria, Egypt, which was part of the Roman Empire. He is known as the Father of Orthodoxy. Do you know what orthodoxy means? It comes from two Greek words. Orthos means right, true, and straight. Doxa means opinion. It refers to true religious beliefs. Athanasius helped Christians understand that Jesus is fully God and fully man. At that time there was a man named Arius who argued that the Father alone was truly God and that the Son was the first and greatest creature made by the Father.
That is not biblical. Athanasius defended the truth even when it was hard. What would it mean if Jesus was not truly God?
